tagline: Two lanes through McKee at the edge of the Cumberland Plateau
intro: KY 89 is a two-lane road through Jackson County, at the edge of the Cumberland Plateau beside Kentucky’s Bluegrass region. McKee lies within the Daniel Boone National Forest, which covers one fourth of the county. Kentucky’s Transportation Cabinet designates a 35.517-mile scenic corridor between KY 490 in Rockcastle County and the Estill County line, using KY 89 and US 421 through McKee.

That scenic designation dates to November 20, 1996. The numbered highway extends farther, running from KY 490 east of Livingston to KY 627 in Winchester. McKee also became a connection to a different kind of route: the Sheltowee Trace, a recreation trail established in 1979, has its centermost trailhead here.

Traveling south from the Estill County line, follow KY 89 into McKee and its Pigeon Roost Creek valley. The scenic corridor uses US 421 through town, then continues on KY 89 to Rockcastle County and the junction with KY 490.

moments.title: Arthur Lakes Log House
moments.text: The Arthur Lakes Log House uses three kinds of wood in successive layers: oak at the bottom, tulip poplar in the middle and pine at the top. Built about 1890 at 401 Lakes Creek Road, the two-room saddlebag house has half-dovetail notching. It entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2000.

moments.title: McKee
moments.text: McKee stands where road routes and a long-distance trail meet: US 421 passes through its center, KY 89 leads north and southwest, and the Sheltowee Trace has its centermost trailhead here. The town occupies Pigeon Roost Creek’s valley within the Daniel Boone National Forest. At the western end of town, Pigeon Roost joins Birch Lick Creek to form Indian Creek, which flows southwest toward the Middle Fork of the Rockcastle River. McKee is Jackson County’s seat and its only city.

moments.title: Cruise
moments.text: Cruise took its name from an early settler and entrepreneur with that surname. A post office opened in 1899, with Welcom Mullins as its first postmaster.

sources.label: Kentucky Transportation Cabinet, Kentucky State and National Scenic Byways and Highways
